How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Patients with low back pain (LBP) often improve during treatment. But some of that improvement would have happened anyway (natural recovery). Some comes from the experience of receiving care (contextual response). Only the rest is due to the treatment itself. We evaluated spinal manipulative therapy (SMT) and common alternatives in two ways: against each other, and against an independent estimate of how LBP improves without treatment (natural history).

We conducted a Bayesian hierarchical network meta-analysis (NMA) of 133 retained analytic units. Acute and chronic LBP were analyzed separately. A companion paper (Paper I) estimated natural history for each phase from separate prognosis studies. We imported those estimates unchanged. No treatment-trial data were used to build them. They served as an external "what would have happened anyway" comparison. The NMA compared SMT, exercise, medical care, NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.

[div-01]

physical modalities, self-care, and sham. We kept two comparisons separate: treatment minus natural history, and treatment minus sham. Uncertainty from both analyses was carried through to the final comparisons.

Results

In acute LBP, natural history predicted that 75.2% of patients would recover by 26 weeks. SMT recovery was 63.2%. That is 12.0 fewer recoveries per 100 than natural history (95% interval -23.2 to -0.7) and 3.1 more per 100 than sham (-6.3 to +12.8). In chronic LBP, where recovery means a favorable course, natural-history recovery at 54 weeks was 18.1%. SMT recovery was 31.8%. That is 13.8 more recoveries per 100 than natural history (+4.3 to +22.6) and 13.4 more than sham (+4.3 to +21.9). Exercise was similar (+12.5 per 100 versus sham; +5.5 to +20.4).

Chronic sham and natural history were nearly identical (+0.4 per 100; -4.2 to +5.7).

Conclusions

Whether an LBP treatment looks effective depends on its comparator. Our linked design keeps the prognosis evidence and the treatment evidence apart until the final comparison. In acute LBP, recovery rates were high, and no treatment added a detectable benefit beyond sham or beyond expected natural recovery. In chronic LBP, SMT and exercise showed some benefit beyond natural history and sham. Even so, only about one in three chronic patients was modeled to recover with either treatment.

Introduction

Low back pain (LBP) is a leading cause of disability and lost work worldwide [1]. In the United States, low back and neck pain accounted for more health-care spending than any other condition, an estimated $134.5 billion in 2016 [2]. Decades of randomized trials and many systematic reviews have failed to settle which conservative treatments work best. Spinal manipulative therapy (SMT), exercise, medical care, physical modalities, education, and selfcare have each been reported superior in some of five decades of studies. Yet the differences among them are inconsistent from one trial or review to the next [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6].

One reason may be simple. Getting better during treatment is not the same as getting better because of treatment. Changes in pain can have several sources. The condition may be improving on its own. Patients often enroll in trials during a flare, and pain tends to drift back toward its usual level afterward (regression to the mean). Patients may also respond to attention, expectation, reassurance, and simply taking part in care. Only the remainder is caused by the treatment itself. Randomized trials can estimate differences between treatment groups. They cannot, by themselves, tell us how much of the improvement within each group would have happened without the treatment [7] [8] [9]. This matters greatly in LBP because the natural course depends on how long the pain has lasted.

Acute episodes often improve a great deal on their own. Chronic LBP improves more slowly and less completely. So, a treatment that looks impressive in acute LBP may add little to recovery that would have happened anyway. The same observed improvement in chronic LBP may mean much more, because it departs further from the expected course. If we pool or interpret treatment effects without modeling this background recovery, we can miss important differences between acute and chronic LBP.

A second problem is the choice of comparator. In this analysis, "sham" means a placebo procedure or a treatment known to be ineffective. Patients who receive sham still improve. That improvement has two parts: the natural course of LBP, and the response to being treated in a clinical or research setting. The NMA compared all treatments with one another. Separately, the independent natural-history estimate showed how much improvement to expect without the treatments being compared. Subtracting natural history from sham (sham minus NH) gave us an estimate of placebo responsiveness.

A third problem is that the trials differ a great deal (heterogeneity). They enroll different patients, follow them for different lengths of time, and deliver treatment at different intensities. Providers come from different professions. Study quality and sham designs vary. Factors such as expectation, confidence, trust, and the patient-provider relationship may matter, but they are rarely measured or reported. These differences can distort both direct and indirect comparisons.

They can also undermine two assumptions that an NMA depends on: transitivity and exchangeability (explained in the Methods). Differences between studies must therefore be modeled directly, not assumed to be differences between treatments.

This study uses a Bayesian hierarchical model and analyzes acute and chronic LBP separately.

The natural-history (NH) trajectories come from a companion meta-analysis (Paper I). Their uncertainty is carried forward into the treatment analysis.

The guiding question is simple: compared with what? Getting better, getting better while being treated, getting better more than expected, and getting better more than with sham are related ideas. But they are not the same causal claim. The analysis therefore has two separate Bayesian parts. Prognosis studies produce the natural-history estimates. Treatment trials produce the treatment estimates. The two meet only at the end, when we compare their posterior distributions directly. Natural history is not added to the network as an extra control arm. Treatment minus natural history and treatment minus sham are different comparisons, and they cannot simply be added together. Paper I estimates the natural-history posteriors [38]. This paper applies them to SMT and its comparators.

Objectives

Our objectives were to: (1) compare SMT with other conservative treatments in separate acute and chronic Bayesian networks; (2) estimate treatment and sham trajectories without using the prognosis evidence; (3) import the natural-history estimates from Paper I and compare treatments with them, but only when both measure the same outcome in the same way; (4) estimate treatment minus sham and sham minus natural history as separate comparisons; and (5) test how robust the results are to study quality, heterogeneity, transitivity, exchangeability, the definition of recovery, and direct versus indirect evidence.

To our knowledge, this is the first SMT analysis to estimate natural recovery independently and carry its uncertainty into a comparison of treatments.

Methods

Study design and analytic framework

We combined comparative studies of conservative treatments for low back pain (LBP) in a Bayesian hierarchical model. Randomized and controlled clinical trials were the main source of evidence. We also kept some prospective observational cohorts when they added useful information about how pain changes over time or how much studies differ. We did not treat these cohorts as if they had been randomized, so we did not assume they were free of confounding.

The analysis was built to separate three parts of observed improvement. The first is improvement expected from the natural course of LBP. The second is improvement from the general experience of receiving care. The third is improvement due to the specific treatment. Acute and chronic LBP were analyzed separately. Their natural courses differ a great deal, and pooling them would mix patients who are not truly comparable.

Dual Bayesian analytic logic

This paper is the second of two linked Bayesian analyses. Paper I combines separate prognosis studies to estimate natural history for each phase of LBP. This paper does not re-estimate those models. Instead, it builds its own Bayesian treatment networks for each phase. It brings in the Paper I results only at the final, interpretive step.

We kept the two evidence streams apart. Treatment trials do not update the natural-history estimate. Sham arms are not relabeled as natural history. Prognosis cohorts are not added to the network as stand-in control arms. Results from the two analyses are combined only when they describe the same clinical outcome. Treatment versus sham is a separate comparison made within the network. This separation matters most for chronic LBP. Chronic pain comes and goes. So "meaningful improvement," "time spent doing well," "pain-free," "remission," "persistence," and "recurrence" are different outcomes. They cannot be swapped for one another. We therefore report treatment minus natural history only when the chronic natural history estimate and the treatment estimate measure the same outcome. Otherwise, they must be linked by an explicit and defensible measurement model. We did this by fitting the chronic treatment model with Paper I's chronic natural-history posterior, in its reference outcome, as the starting line (see Outcomes).

The final evidence set had 133 analytic units from 131 parent trials. (An analytic unit is a study, or a separable part of a study, that contributes data.) Of these, 59 contributed acute data and 74 contributed chronic data. Three units contributed to both. That gives 130 unique units assigned to a phase. Kinalski [39] had mixed or unknown phase and was not assigned to either analysis. Sturion [40] was kept to document its design before crossover, but it gave no separate treatment estimate we could use. Licciardone [41] reported a single cross-sectional pain score at registry enrollment, with no follow-up, so it gave no longitudinal estimate and was kept in the inventory only. Each observation was identified by study, treatment category (the T6 variable), and week of follow-up. Each study was assigned to the acute or chronic phase. Acute observations were modeled through 26 weeks and chronic observations through 54 weeks. Table 1 summarizes treatments by phase. Table 2 specifies the Bayesian model. Table 3 accounts for every unit in the evidence base. The retained evidence base comprised 131 parent trials represented by 133 analytic units; inventory reconciliation is reported separately in Table 3.

Natural Historychronic

Natural-course/prognosis evidence only: 12 cohorts / 15 observations at all reported follow-up times (54 weeks is the reporting horizon, not an eligibility rule). logit p(t)=theta54+beta*[log(1+t)-log(1+54)]+alpha_family+u[cohort]; outcome-family offsets for STRICT and COURSE definitions, DIRECT is the reference family. Posterior means: theta54=-1.561, beta=0.176, alpha_strict=0.455, alpha_course=0.368, sigma_u=0.857. This posterior is the chronic treatment model's external NH offset, entered on the g scale as qnorm(p_NH(t))+DELTA_CHRONIC before treatment effects are estimated; chronic treatment probabilities are p_k=Phi(qnorm(p_NH)+tx_effect_k).

Treatment effects

Six categories: sham, SMT, exercise, medical care, modalities, and self-care. tx_effect[k] is the time-invariant additive deviation from Natural History and is modeled hierarchically as Normal(0,sigma_tx^2).

SMT provider effects

Provider effects use the non-centered hierarchy gamma[p]=z_gamma[p]*sigma_prov for PT, DC, DO, MD, Bonesetters, and Mixed; non-SMT observations use the neutral provider code.

Study effects u[study] ~ Normal(0,tau^2). Treatment-by-study effects use the non-centered hierarchy v[k,j]=z_v[k,j]*sigma_tx_x_study.

Covariates

Centered log(sample size) and centered PEDro score; beta_n and beta_q ~ Normal(0,1). PEDro is a covariate/sensitivity variable, not an exclusion criterion.

Scale priors sigma_tx, sigma_prov, tau, sigma_tx_x_study, and sigma_resid use half-t(df=1, scale=0.5) priors.

TECHNICAL DETAILS

Treatment-model MCMC JAGS via rjags; 4 chains. Acute: 5,000 adaptation + 35,000 burn-in + 150,000 sampling, thin=4. Chronic: 4,000 adaptation + 35,000 burn-in + 150,000 sampling, thin=4. Fresh-sample retry is triggered if max PSRF exceeds 1.01. Counting identity: 59 acute + 74 chronic -3 analytic units represented in both phases + 1 mixed/unknown unassigned quantitative unit(s) + 1 retained unit(s) without a separable quantitative estimate + 1 retained cross-sectional unit(s) without a longitudinal estimate = 133 retained analytic units.

NH-model MCMC

JAGS

Acute and chronic treatment-category study counts include mixed-population studies assigned to that phase. The Mixed-population studies column makes those studies explicit rather than treating Kinalski_1989 as the only mixed study.

PEDro is summarized once per analytic unit; if duplicate source rows disagree, the unit-level median is used before calculating the phase-by-treatment mean and SD.

No genuine week-0 observations were available in the quantitative treatment data. The sample-size column is therefore labeled Initial / earliest reported N: within each phase, analytic unit, and treatment, sample size is taken at the earliest recorded week and is not presented as a week-0 baseline count. Sham is the randomized sham or therapeutically inactive comparator category and is not one of the five active treatment categories requested in this table.

Literature search for treatment studies

We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. We also used resources from the University of Arizona Health Sciences Library.

Searches combined terms for LBP with terms for spinal manipulation and related manual treatments. To find trials, we added terms for randomized or controlled clinical trials. We also checked the reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews.

The main PubMed MeSH terms were Manipulation, Spinal, Manipulation, Chiropractic, Manipulation, Osteopathic, Musculoskeletal Manipulations, Low Back Pain, Back Pain, Lumbosacral Region, and Sciatica. We added free-text terms: spinal manipulation, chiropractic manipulation, osteopathic manipulation or osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT), manual therapy, mobilization/mobilisation, spinal adjustment, thrust, high-velocity low-amplitude or HVLA manipulation, flexion-distraction, low back pain, lumbar pain, lumbago, lumbosacral pain, and sciatica. Trial terms were randomized/randomised, controlled clinical trial, placebo, sham, trial, and groups. In the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), we did not add a trial filter, because that database contains only controlled trials. We adapted the search terms to each database's syntax and indexing.

The evidence base was built up over time. We added studies through citation searching and relevant systematic reviews. The exact wording of every early search was not saved. The search strategy described here therefore records the concepts we used to build and update the database.

It does not claim that one identical search string was run at every stage. The treatment evidence included studies of acute LBP [39, and chronic LBP [15, 40, 41, 45, 49,. Studies that contributed to both phases are listed in both groups.

Search criteria in brief. Databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, and Google Scholar, supplemented by University of Arizona Health Sciences Library resources and backward and forward citation searching of included studies and systematic reviews. Search structure: (low back pain terms) AND (spinal manipulation and manual-therapy terms) AND (randomized or controlled trial terms), using the MeSH and free-text terms listed above; no trial filter was applied in CENTRAL. Period: searches were run repeatedly between 2009 and 2026 as the evidence base was built and updated. Eligible studies: randomized or controlled clinical trials of adults with acute or chronic low back pain that included spinal manipulation or another conservative treatment (exercise, medical care, physical modalities, self-care) or a sham or inactive comparator, and that reported pain intensity at baseline and at least one follow-up in a form convertible to the common standardized scale, with arm sample sizes. Analysis windows: acute observations up to 26 weeks and chronic observations up to 54 weeks. Prospective observational cohorts were eligible only for information on change over time, as described below.

Eligibility and study classification

We included randomized or controlled clinical trials of adults with LBP. When they added useful information, we also included prospective observational cohorts. Every study had to report a pain outcome we could convert to our common scale. Treatment arms were sorted into six categories: spinal manipulation therapy (SMT), exercise, medical care, physical modalities, self-care, and sham. Sham meant a placebo procedure or a treatment known to be ineffective. We classified each arm by what was done, not by who did it. So manipulation by a chiropractor, osteopath, physician, or physiotherapist counted as SMT if it included spinal manipulation or a similar thrust procedure. Multi-part osteopathic manipulative treatments stayed in the SMT category.

Where needed, we flagged them separately for sensitivity and transitivity checks.

Observational studies were used only for purposes their design could support. We assumed their data on how pain changes over time could stand in for the trial populations, once we accounted for clinical phase, follow-up time, differences between studies, and measured design features.

Their outcomes also had to fit our common recovery scale, and the timing of their measurements had to be clear. These assumptions are about how pain changes over time. They are not about who received which treatment. So we did not use observational cohorts to estimate treatment effects when there was no proper comparison group. Nor did we treat a treated cohort as if it were untreated natural history. Ailliet (2018) and Leemann (2014) are two prospective cohorts kept for their data on change over time, under these limits [15, 49]. Ailliet (2018) enrolled patients with neck pain or LBP; we extracted only the LBP subgroup (n = 295), using class-sizeweighted means across its four LBP trajectory classes at baseline, 26 weeks and 52 weeks.

Some studies enrolled both acute and chronic patients. We kept these when the two groups could be separated. Acute data went into the acute analysis and chronic data into the chronic analysis.

If a study's phase could not be assigned reliably, it stayed in the inventory but was left out of both models. Studies were excluded only because of their population, treatment, design, missing outcomes, or data that could not be mapped to our outcome. They were never excluded because of the direction or size of their results.

Outcome extraction and standardization

Pain was the main outcome. Numerical rating scale (NRS) and visual analogue scale (VAS) scores were converted to a common 0-100 scale before we calculated standardized change.

Many studies measured pain more than once during follow-up. We kept each follow-up as a separate time point within its original arm or cohort. We did not count repeated measurements as extra arms or extra patients [164].

To describe how severe pain was at enrollment, we also put baseline pain on a 0-10 scale. Scores already on a 0-10 scale were kept. Scores on a 0-100 scale were divided by 10. Each physical arm's baseline was counted only once. Arm means were weighted by the number of patients enrolled to get summaries by study, treatment, and phase. This baseline description was not used to define treatment effects.

Improvement was expressed as Hedges' g [165]. This is the change in pain divided by the pooled baseline standard deviation. It puts studies that used different pain scales on the same footing.

Positive values mean improvement. Each study kept its identifier throughout. That way, repeated measurements and multiple arms from one study were not treated as if they came from separate studies.

We also converted improvement into the chance of recovery, because that is easier to interpret clinically. Our main definition of recovery was pain of 2/10 or less. The conversion was calibrated separately for each phase. Average starting pain, weighted by sample size, was 4.823/10 in acute LBP and 5.284/10 in chronic LBP. We used a fixed standard deviation of 2.0 NRS points (SD_NRS = 2.0). To reach 2/10, patients therefore needed to drop 2.823 points (acute) or 3.284 points (chronic). In standardized units, these thresholds are Δ = 1.412 (acute) and Δ = 1.642 (chronic). The chance of recovery was P(recovery) = Φ(g -Δ_phase), where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function [166, 167]. This is a model-based translation of average improvement into a recovery rate. It is not a directly counted proportion of recovered patients. The baseline means and the SD were treated as fixed values, not as uncertain quantities. The 2/10 threshold was set in advance [168]. Chronic LBP was handled differently. Paper I's chronic natural-history model estimates the probability of a favorable course at 54 weeks, using its reference (DIRECT) outcome family. A favorable course is not the same as pain of 2/10 or less. So for chronic LBP the natural-history posterior entered the treatment model directly, as its starting line on the g scale, where effect_k is that treatment's standardized deviation from natural history.

In chronic LBP, "recovery" therefore means a favorable course. We also tested three other definitions of recovery: any improvement, at least 30% reduction, and at least 50% reduction.

For each posterior draw s, recovery and the treatment-minus-sham difference are calculated as follows: where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function; g is standardized mean improvement; Δphase is the phase-specific standardized recovery threshold (acute 1.412; chronic 1.642); s indexes posterior draws; gNH(s) is the natural history value in draw s; pNH(s), pk(s), and psham(s) are the recovery probabilities for natural history, treatment k, and sham, respectively; θk(s) is the standardized treatment effect for treatment k in draw s; and Dk,sham(s) is the treatment-minus-sham difference in recoveries per 100 persons.

In plain terms, g is how far the average patient in an arm has moved, in baseline standard deviations. Δ is how far a patient must move to cross the recovery line, from the average starting pain down to 2/10. Suppose individual changes are roughly bell-shaped around the arm average, with the same SD used for standardizing. Then Φ(g -Δ) is the share of patients expected to cross the line. In acute LBP, Δ = 1.412. An arm that improves by g = 1.0 (about 2 NRS points) gives Φ(-0.41) ≈ 34% recovered. An arm that improves by g = 0.5 gives about 18%. The threshold is essential. Without it, Φ(g) would count almost any average improvement as recovery. For example, g = 1.0 would give 84%, turning a modest effect into near-certain success. Because the conversion relies on a distributional assumption, it is a model-based estimate, not an observed count. The four recovery definitions in the sensitivity analysis show how much the conclusions depend on it [166, 167].

The natural-history and treatment posteriors come from separate evidence. So we paired their draws at random to simulate their joint distribution (Monte Carlo sampling). We calculated posterior means and credible intervals only after converting each draw to a recovery probability.

The order matters because Φ is a curve, not a straight line. The average of converted values is not the same as converting the average. Suppose natural-history uncertainty came down to just two equally likely draws: g = 0 and g = 1.0. In acute LBP, these give recovery rates of 7.9% and 34.0%, which average 21%. If we average g first (0.5) and then convert, we get 18%. Converting each draw and then summarizing keeps the full uncertainty in the result. Converting a single point estimate quietly throws it away [169]. Pairing the draws at random is valid here because the two posteriors share no data. It would be wrong if the same trials had informed both.

Study quality

Each randomized study received a single rating on the PEDro quality scale. Ratings were made with the assistance of an artificial intelligence model (ChatGPT). They were not duplicated and were not checked against ratings by human reviewers.

PEDro was designed for randomized trials. For nonrandomized studies, we therefore described design and source separately rather than forcing them onto the PEDro scale. PEDro entered both treatment models as a standardized study-level covariate, so its coefficient is the change in improvement per 1 SD of PEDro score; studies without a score were set to the mean. PEDro was also used in sensitivity analyses. It was not used to exclude studies.

External natural-history posterior from linked Paper I

Paper I estimated natural history on its own, using separate prognosis studies. Paper I defines the outcomes for each phase, the sources, how chronic outcomes were judged, the Bayesian models, where y_i is standardized within-arm improvement for observation i; mu_i is its treatment-model expectation; SE_i is its within-observation standard error; theta[k] is the treatment-category effect; gamma[p] is an SMT-provider deviation where applicable; u[j] is a study random effect; and v[k,j] is a treatment-by-study deviation.

The independent natural-history posterior is introduced only after this treatment model has produced posterior draws.

Each term in the model soaks up a different source of variation, so that it is not mistaken for a treatment effect. θ[k] is the quantity we care about: the average improvement for treatment category k. u[j] lets each study sit higher or lower overall. This reflects its patients, setting, and measures. All arms in a study share u[j], so comparisons within a study are not affected by it.

v[k,j] lets a treatment do somewhat better or worse in one study than on average. This is how the model captures trial-to-trial variation in the treatment effect itself. γ[p] lets SMT delivered by different types of provider differ from the SMT average. The log(n) and PEDro terms adjust for patterns linked to small studies and to study quality. SE_i² carries each observation's own sampling uncertainty. σ_resid² adds variance when the data scatter more than their reported standard errors predict. As in the chronic natural-history model of Paper I, these random effects let studies differ without letting those differences pose as treatment effects.

We used two reference comparisons. Treatment versus natural history compares modeled recovery on treatment with the independently estimated course of untreated LBP. Treatment versus sham compares one treatment with sham inside the network. These answer different questions. They are not parts that add up to a total. We estimated placebo responsiveness as sham minus natural history, which removes the recovery expected anyway.

Placebo responsiveness = sham -natural history

We ran the network meta-analysis separately for the acute and chronic networks, using the six treatment categories. Trials with more than two arms kept their within-study structure. We report posterior means and 95% credible intervals (CrIs). A standardized effect of about ±0.30 served as a rough guide to clinical importance. It was a reference zone, not a pass/fail test of significance [168, 170].

Absolute-recovery benchmark and posterior decision probability

For each treatment, we asked: in what share of posterior draws did the modeled recovery rate exceed 50%? This tells us how sure we are about the population recovery rate, given the model, the outcome definition, and the follow-up time. It is not the chance that a given patient benefits from treatment. It is not the share of patients whose improvement was caused by treatment. And it is not the size of the treatment effect. The 50% benchmark is also different from three other cut-offs used in this paper: the individual recovery definition (pain ≤2/10), the 50% painreduction definition used in sensitivity analyses, and the ±0.30 reference zone for effect size. The benchmark is not a validated policy threshold. We calculated these probabilities from the saved posterior draws at each phase's endpoint.

Two probabilities are easy to confuse here. The chance that the population recovery rate exceeds 50% describes our certainty. It does not describe patients. Imagine a treatment with a modeled recovery of 55% and a narrow interval. Its chance of exceeding the benchmark could be above 90%. Yet only about 55 of 100 patients would be expected to recover. The posterior says nothing about which patients recover, or whether treatment caused it. In contrast, a treatment with a modeled recovery of 45% and a wide interval might have a 30% chance of exceeding the benchmark (hypothetical values). The first number is confidence about a population value. The second is the population value itself.

Transitivity, exchangeability, and network assumptions

We checked transitivity and exchangeability separately in the acute and chronic networks. (Both are explained below.) We compared possible effect modifiers across treatment comparisons.

These included clinical phase, follow-up time, baseline pain, sample size, study quality, treatment category, provider type where known, and other available study features. We displayed these checks as grids of plots (lattices) for each phase. This let us look for imbalance across many features at once, rather than judging one covariate at a time.

We also assessed exchangeability through differences between studies, study-level random effects, residual patterns, the link between treatment and quality, and sensitivity analyses. Where studies overlapped little on these features, we interpreted direct and indirect evidence with caution. These checks show whether the assumptions are plausible. They do not prove that transitivity holds.

An indirect comparison works through a shared comparator. Suppose SMT beats sham by g = 0.2 in one set of trials, and exercise beats sham by g = 0.1 in another. The network then infers that SMT beats exercise by about 0.1 (hypothetical values). That inference holds only if both sets of sham-controlled trials enrolled similar patients. Only then is sham the same yardstick in each. If the SMT trials had enrolled milder or more recent cases, the indirect estimate would compare patient groups as well as treatments. Transitivity is the assumption that the yardstick is shared.

Exchangeability is the closely related assumption that the trials are similar enough to be combined. The lattice plots check whether measured effect modifiers are spread evenly enough across comparisons for these assumptions to be plausible [171].

Direct and indirect evidence as an NMA validity check

Before interpreting the network estimates, we checked whether the evidence could support valid indirect comparisons. We first confirmed that the network was connected and reviewed the transitivity and exchangeability checks described above. We then used standard random-effects NMA diagnostics. These looked at differences between studies, overall inconsistency, and local agreement between direct and indirect evidence. We checked local inconsistency by node splitting. This compares the effect estimated from head-to-head trials with the effect estimated indirectly through the rest of the network [171] [172] [173].

We treated these checks as a requirement for interpreting the NMA, not as optional extras. We looked closely at how large and how uncertain any direct-indirect disagreement was. We also noted whether each comparison rested mainly on direct or indirect evidence. A non-significant inconsistency test was not taken as proof of consistency, especially when a comparison had little data. Where direct and indirect estimates disagreed, or where effect modifiers overlapped little, we interpreted the network estimate more cautiously.

Take modalities versus SMT as an example. The network has two kinds of evidence for this pair.

Some trials compared the two head-to-head. Other evidence comes indirectly, through other treatments. Node splitting estimates the comparison from each source separately and asks whether they agree. Agreement supports combining them. Disagreement suggests that some trials differ in ways that break the shared-yardstick assumption. When a comparison has little data, both routes give wide intervals. So failing to find disagreement is only weak evidence that the two sources agree [174].

Leakage and independence audit

We brought in natural history on purpose as outside evidence. So we audited study names and sources to make sure no study appeared in both the natural-history set and the treatment network.

We checked exact names and sources to catch duplicates. Reviews that included cohorts already used in the natural-history model were not added as extra natural-history studies. Sham arms from the treatment network were not used to build the natural-history trajectory. This kept information from the treatment trials out of the benchmark used to judge those same trials.

Independence matters for a simple reason. If the same trials had helped build the natural-history benchmark and were then judged against it, the benchmark would be partly made from the results it is meant to test. Those trials would be pulled toward agreeing with it. Treatment-versusnatural-history differences would then shrink toward zero by design. This is the same error as using one dataset both to pick a hypothesis and to test it, sometimes called "double dipping" [175]. Keeping the two evidence streams apart means the benchmark was fixed before we looked at the treatment data.

Sensitivity and validation analyses

Sensitivity analyses tested other natural-history models, the recovery threshold, assumptions about treatment rates, study quality, blinding, and the line between natural history and shamrelated improvement. Common-asymptote checks asked whether, in acute LBP, treatments might differ only in how fast patients reach the same end point. This check assumed a shared Bayesian hierarchical natural-history end point, with study as a random factor.

The main sensitivity analyses covered: the definition of recovery; two methods for translating treatment time (model-based versus the older method); node-splitting at 12 versus 26 weeks in acute LBP (chronic stayed at 54 weeks); reconciling scales; sanity checks in clinical units; and meta-regression on study quality and blinding. We treated the PEDro-based blinding analysis as a rough proxy for overall study quality. That is because PEDro combines blinding with allocation, dropout, intention-to-treat, and other design features.

Paper I reports a linear-form sensitivity analysis for the acute natural-history trajectory; under that form, natural recovery at 26 weeks was 79.9%, compared with 75.2% under the main saturating (leveling-off) form. We therefore reran the full acute treatment model using the linearform natural-history posterior. This rerun used the same 220 treatment observations, 46 studies, and treatment categories as the main model, so it isolates the effect of curve shape. We compared treatment-versus-sham conclusions directly with the main model (Table 9).

Bayesian computation and convergence

Models were fitted by Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) in JAGS, with four chains per model [176]. All preset convergence criteria were met before results were carried forward. The maximum potential scale reduction factor (PSRF) was 1.0007 (acute) and 1.0026 (chronic) for the treatment models, and 1.0034 and 1.0029 for the natural-history models [177, 178]. Values this close to 1.0 mean the chains agreed. Iteration counts, thinning, minimum effective sample sizes, and retry rules are in Table 2.

Results

Evidence base

The final evidence base had 133 analytic units from 131 parent trials. Fifty-nine units went into the acute analysis and 74 into the chronic analysis. Three units gave separable data to both. That leaves 130 unique units assigned to a phase. Studies that enrolled both acute and chronic patients were kept when the two groups could be separated. Their data went into the right analysis instead of being dropped as mixed. Kinalski (1989) [39] was the only unit whose phase could not be assigned, so it entered neither model. Sturion (2020) [40] stayed in the inventory but gave no separate treatment estimate. Licciardone (2020) reported only a single cross-sectional pain score, so it also stayed in the inventory without a longitudinal estimate. These categories add up exactly to the 133 units. Table 1 summarizes treatments, Table 2 specifies the model, and Table 3 accounts for every unit by phase.

Both treatment networks were connected. That is, every treatment could be linked to every other through some chain of trials. In the network display, SMT had 68 acute and 74 chronic arms.

Head-to-head evidence was strongest for modalities versus SMT (23 analytic study units) and medical care versus SMT (20) in acute LBP. In chronic LBP, it was strongest for sham versus SMT (27), exercise versus SMT (24), modalities versus SMT (20), and medical care versus SMT (18). Figure 1 shows the network, and Table 4 summarizes the head-to-head evidence.

NMA validity: direct and indirect evidence

Before interpreting treatment effects, we checked whether each network met the assumptions needed to combine direct and indirect evidence. Both networks were connected. Measured effect modifiers were similar enough across comparisons to support exchangeability, but only conditionally, not without limits. We then used standard random-effects diagnostics to look at differences between studies, overall inconsistency, and local agreement between direct and indirect evidence [171] [172] [173] 179].

We examined node-splitting results one comparison at a time, rather than relying on P values alone. Comparisons with many trials rested mostly on head-to-head evidence. Comparisons with few trials leaned more on indirect routes through shared comparators. We used the size and uncertainty of any disagreement to temper our interpretation. Figure 2 shows each comparison that had both direct and indirect evidence. Table 4 gives the number of analytic units behind each head-to-head pair. The standard 12-week acute network showed moderate heterogeneity (τ ≈ 0.13; I² ≈ 27%). The chronic 54-week network showed more (τ ≈ 0.34; I² ≈ 73%). Here τ is the standard deviation of true effects across studies, and I² is the share of total variation due to real differences between studies rather than chance. Both point to caution when reading individual comparisons. Table 4. Natural-history trajectories

The natural-history estimates come from Paper I. The acute estimate drew on 8 studies ( 26observations). The chronic estimate drew on 12 cohorts (15 observations). Table 5 lists the sources. Modeled natural-history recovery was 75.2% (95% CrI 49.8% to 94.3%) at 26 weeks in acute LBP. In chronic LBP, the probability of a favorable course at 54 weeks was 18.1% (8.8% to 31.9%).

Paper I models and documents how the natural-history studies differ from one another. This paper takes the resulting posterior as given and does not refit the prognosis data. Figure 3 shows the Paper I natural-history curves alongside the treatment curves.

In acute LBP, no treatment arm did better than natural history. Per 100 patients, differences from natural history ranged from -12.0 for SMT (95% interval -23.2 to -0.7) to -20.7 for exercise (-33.7 to -5.3), and every interval lay below zero. Compared with sham in the network, SMT gave 3.1 more recoveries per 100 (95% interval -6.3 to +12.8). Medical care, exercise, modalities, and self-care ranged from -5.7 to -1.3 per 100. So recovery during acute treatment was high, but natural recovery was even higher. We found no clear treatment-specific signal on top of it. Table 6 gives the exact estimates.

Every acute arm, sham included, fell below natural history. It is unlikely that every treatment, including sham, slows recovery. A more likely explanation is that trial patients and naturalhistory cohorts differ in systematic ways. Trials enroll people who seek care and who meet severity and duration criteria, often during a flare. Trial eligibility rules, such as a minimum pain score, can also exclude people with the mildest pain, who tend to recover fastest; inception and community cohorts include them [180]. Differences in when and how outcomes are measured can add to this gap. The treatment-versus-natural-history comparison therefore mixes any treatment effect with a difference between populations. That is one reason we also report treatment versus sham within the network, where this problem does not arise. The similar pattern of improvement across very different treatments matches earlier findings [7].

The comparisons with natural history at the reporting horizons also rest on a modeling Natural History is the independent external natural-course/prognosis reference. Sham is the randomized sham or therapeutically inactive comparator category. Placebo responsiveness is defined separately as sham minus natural history. Week 12 lies within the observed trial follow-up in both phases; the horizon values extend the fitted treatment effects beyond most trial observations (see Figure 3). Using sham instead of natural history as the comparator led to the same conclusion for acute LBP. Standardized treatment-versus-sham effects were small and uncertain: SMT g = 0.09 (95% CrI -0.18 to 0.35), exercise g = -0.16 (-0.45 to 0.13), modalities g = -0.07 (-0.35 to 0.20), self-care g = -0.04 (-0.36 to 0.28), and medical care g = -0.06 (-0.33 to 0.21). Figure 4 shows these standardized effects alongside the same results per 100 patients. Table 7 gives the full acute model summary.

Why are absolute recovery rates so uncertain while differences between treatments are much sharper? Because every treatment's modeled recovery in Table 6 is built on the same naturalhistory draw: p_k(s) = Φ[g_NH(s) + θ_k(s) -Δ]. In a draw where natural history is favorable, all arms are high. In a draw where it is unfavorable, all are low. That shared uncertainty is why each absolute interval runs from roughly 25% to 90%. When we subtract one arm from another within the same draw, most of the shared part cancels out. What remains is uncertainty about the treatment difference itself. For example, the SMT-versus-sham interval spans about 19 points rather than 56. So wide absolute intervals and narrower differences do not conflict. They answer different questions. In chronic LBP, modeled recovery (a favorable course) at 54 weeks was 18.1% for natural history (95% CrI 8.8% to 31.9%). It ranged from 18.5% for sham to 31.8% for SMT. Per 100 patients, SMT gave 13.8 more recoveries than natural history (95% interval +4.3 to +22.6), exercise 12.9 more (+5.7 to +20.9), and modalities 6.6 more (+0.2 to +14.5). The intervals for medical care (+4.3; -2.5 to +13.1) and self-care (+6.3; -3.0 to +18.7) included zero. Compared with sham, only SMT (+13.4; +4.3 to +21.9) and exercise (+12.5; +5.5 to +20.4) had intervals that excluded zero. Modalities (+6.2; -0.5 to +13.9), self-care (+5.9; -4.0 to +18.1), and medical care (+3.9; -3.9 to +12.9) were uncertain. No treatment reached 50% average recovery. Table 8 gives the full chronic model summary. Treatment effects were smaller against sham than against natural history. In chronic LBP, sham and natural history were nearly identical (+0.4 recoveries per 100; 95% interval -4.2 to +5.7).

We read this difference as placebo responsiveness: the extra improvement from receiving sham, after removing the recovery expected anyway. It reflects the patient's response, not a property of the sham itself. Here it was close to zero. SMT and exercise showed the clearest effects beyond sham. But the active treatments overlapped a great deal, so the data do not support a firm ranking. 9).

Sensitivity to the definition of clinically meaningful recovery

Across all four definitions, the active treatments stayed close together in acute LBP. This supports reading the results separately by phase. It also warns against ranking treatments by posterior means alone.

Together, Figures 3 4 5separate overall prognosis from the advantage of one treatment over another. Figure 3 shows absolute recovery over time for natural history and each treatment.

Figure 4 shows modeled recovery along with differences from natural history and from sham.

Natural history, contextual effects, and treatment-specific effects

The pattern of comparisons differed by phase. In acute LBP, natural history was more favorable than the treatment arms at 26 weeks. Sham fell below natural history (-15.0 per 100; -27.7 to -2.1). Treatment-versus-sham differences were close to zero. In chronic LBP, active treatments were above natural history. Sham was essentially equal to it (+0.4 per 100; -4.2 to +5.7). This pattern lets us separate background prognosis from the added effect of treatment. It also lets us read sham minus natural history as placebo responsiveness, after removing the recovery expected anyway.

This placebo response may reflect expectation, the patient-provider relationship, reassurance, attention, conditioning, the ritual of treatment, provider interaction, and other effects of receiving a sham or ineffective treatment in a clinical or research setting. This analysis does not separate these mechanisms.

The overall pattern is best stated with care. In acute LBP, improvement happens against a very favorable natural course, and treatment adds little beyond sham. In chronic LBP, improvement happens against a less favorable natural course, and SMT and exercise show the clearest added effects beyond sham. Large improvements within treatment arms and modest differences between treatments can therefore exist side by side in the same evidence.

Study quality and blinding

In acute LBP, studies with higher PEDro scores showed more improvement across all their arms (0.291 per SD; 95% CrI 0.042 to 0.524). In chronic LBP, the PEDro term was small and uncertain (0.052; -0.119 to 0.219). Because this term shifts each study's overall level, it does not change comparisons between treatments within a study. Exploratory analyses of quality and blinding did not find a stable link between study quality and treatment differences. Estimates for different SMT provider types were also imprecise. Every 95% credible interval included zero in both acute and chronic LBP. So we found no consistent differences in SMT results by provider type. But overlapping intervals do not prove that providers are equivalent. Variation between providers was smaller than variation between studies (acute provider SD 0.114 versus τ 0.627; chronic 0.143 versus 0.433). Treatment-by-study and residual variation were smaller still.

The six acute provider estimates in Table 7 range only from 61.6% to 64.9%. That narrow range is partly a product of partial pooling. The model estimates how much providers truly differ (provider SD 0.114, interval from near zero to 0.373). It then pulls each provider's estimate toward the SMT average. The less data a provider has, the stronger the pull. When the estimated spread is small and provider data are sparse, the estimates end up close together. So nearly identical provider estimates mean the data cannot tell providers apart. They do not show that providers are the same [181].

Transitivity, exchangeability, and model assumptions

We analyzed the acute and chronic networks separately. Their background recovery differs too much to assume the two populations are exchangeable. Within each phase, measured effect modifiers overlapped enough to support exchangeability, but only conditionally. Direct and indirect estimates generally agreed. The main local inconsistency was modalities versus SMT in the acute network (P = 0.039). We found no local inconsistency in the chronic network. We treated sparse comparisons and leftover heterogeneity as reasons for caution, not as grounds to assume the studies were fully exchangeable.

No single measured covariate showed a broad failure of transitivity. Leftover differences between studies were handled by study-level random effects. We read the network estimates as average effects across trials that differ but overlap enough to combine. The direct-indirect comparisons in Figure 2 give an empirical check on consistency. The audit of clinical and design features supports exchangeability only conditionally.

Sensitivity to the imported natural-history posterior

Under the linear-form acute natural-history posterior from Paper I, natural recovery at 26 weeks was 79.9% (95% CrI 53.8% to 95.7%), compared with 75.2% under the main saturating model.

The active-treatment comparisons with sham hardly moved. SMT versus sham was g = 0.083 (95% CrI -0.179 to 0.346) under the linear model. Under the main saturating model, it was g = 0.087 (95% CrI -0.177 to 0.351). All other treatment-versus-sham intervals included zero under both models (Table 9; Figure 6).

In the acute common-asymptote sensitivity model (233 observations from 55 studies, fitted with lme4), treatments could speed up or slow down recovery but had to share the natural-history start and endpoint. Sham and every active treatment except self-care recovered more slowly than natural history. Rate shifts versus natural history were: sham -0.47 (95% CI -0.63 to -0.30), SMT -0.39 (-0.52 to -0.25), exercise -0.51 (-0.72 to -0.30), medical care -0.70 (-0.96 to -0.45), modalities -0.46 (-0.63 to -0.28), and self-care -0.34 (-0.82 to 0.15). Modeled recovery at 4 weeks was 63.9% for natural history against 22.9% to 43.2% across trial arms. By 12 weeks the gap had narrowed to under 5 points (natural history 76.7%; trial arms 72.4% to 74.7%), and at 26 weeks modeled recovery was 77.1% in every trial arm and 77.2% for natural history.

We also fitted a free-ceiling version of this model, in which each arm could differ from natural history both in its speed of recovery and in the level at which it leveled off. Letting the ceiling vary fitted the data far better than forcing convergence (AIC 319.8 versus 465.4; likelihood-ratio χ² = 157.6, 6 df, P < 0.001), and every arm's ceiling lay below natural history (for example, SMT -1.05 g, 95% CI -1.21 to -0.89). Over the observed follow-up, then, the gap between trial arms and natural history did not close. The size of that gap, however, depended on the model. The free-ceiling model, which lacks the primary model's treatment-by-study random effects and holds natural history at its posterior-mean curve, gave much larger gaps and implausible shapes, with sham recovery rising to 27.2% at 4 weeks and then falling. We therefore take the primary model's within-trial estimates as the more conservative measure of the gap, and draw from the time-shape analyses only the conclusions they share: trial arms recover more slowly than natural history early, and the gap persists through the observed follow-up.
