These results show that absolute recovery is sensitive to the natural-history model, but comparisons between treatments are not. Acute sensitivity to curve shape is reported here, using Other recovery definitions, treatment-time translations, acute node-splitting time points, scale reconciliation, and common-asymptote checks did not change the main conclusions. Acute LBP showed fast background recovery and little treatment-versus-sham difference. Chronic LBP showed slower natural recovery, with SMT and exercise giving the clearest added benefit over sham. Figure 5 shows that the acute treatment-versus-sham conclusions hold under all four recovery definitions.

Discussion

Principal Findings

This analysis helps explain a long-standing puzzle in the low back pain (LBP) literature. Patients usually get better, yet it has been hard to show which treatment is responsible. Much of the puzzle goes away once three quantities are kept apart. They are often blurred together. The first is absolute recovery: how many patients get better. The second is improvement beyond the expected natural course. The third is improvement beyond sham. This is a counterfactual analysis, not a ranking of treatments. The question is not whether patients improved but compared with what. Natural history and treatment were each estimated as full probability distributions. So the result compares two distributions, rather than subtracting one point estimate from another [38].

The answer depended strongly on how long the pain had lasted. In acute LBP, natural history showed fast improvement. Recovery rates on treatment were high. But once this background recovery was considered, little extra improvement was left for treatment. Effects relative to natural history were mostly negative or near zero. Effects relative to sham were near zero, with wide uncertainty. Acute LBP thus shows that a good outcome does not mean a large treatment effect. Many patients recover while being treated, even when little of that recovery is due to the treatment.

The acute shortfall against natural history should not be read as proof that treatment slows recovery. No treatment, not even sham, recovered faster than natural history. On average, treated arms were somewhat slower (Table 6). The common-asymptote rate model points the same way.

Three features of the evidence argue against a causal reading. First, sham also fell below natural history, and no active treatment beat sham. So, the shortfall is shared by all trial arms and cannot be pinned on any one treatment. Second, the comparison is between trial arms and outside cohorts, not a randomized comparison. Trial patients are care-seekers selected for pain severity and duration, and outcome definitions differ between trials and cohorts. Third, the size of the shortfall depends on which curve shape is assumed for acute natural history (Table 9). A true causal effect of treatment would not. These data cannot tell whether the shortfall comes from trial participation, the selection of care-seekers, or treatment itself (for example, by making patients feel more ill, or through nocebo effects).

Chronic LBP showed the opposite pattern. Natural history predicted much slower and less complete recovery (18.1% at 54 weeks). Absolute recovery was therefore lower than in acute LBP. SMT, exercise, and modalities beat natural history, and SMT and exercise showed the clearest benefit over sham. Placebo responsiveness (sham minus natural history) was close to zero (+0.4 per 100; -4.2 to +5.7). In chronic LBP, then, receiving sham added little beyond the expected course. Absolute prognosis and the comparative effect of treatment remain two different things.

Why has the SMT literature stayed so mixed? Our findings suggest that the answer differs between acute and chronic LBP. In acute LBP, fast natural improvement creates a large background signal. Small treatment-specific differences must be detected against it. So, a large improvement in an SMT arm is not, by itself, evidence that SMT works. Repeated trials may keep producing favorable, null, or unfavorable results, depending on chance, the comparator, and the follow-up time. In chronic LBP, natural recovery is weaker, so a treatment signal is easier to see. Here, SMT and exercise showed the clearest advantage over sham. This acute-chronic difference may explain why the SMT literature remains inconclusive. It also closely matches an earlier comparative-effectiveness analysis. In that study, nonspecific factors explained most acute improvement, while treatment explained a larger share of chronic outcomes [182]. Even in chronic LBP, though, modeled recovery at 54 weeks stayed below 50% (SMT 31.8%; exercise 30.9%), with wide uncertainty.

Natural history and the Interpretation of Treatment Response

Most treatment studies assume natural history rather than estimate it. Randomization protects the comparison between groups from many biases. But it does not show that the improvement within either group was caused by the treatment. When a condition improves quickly on its own, a treatment can look very successful in a before-and-after or within-group analysis, even when its added effect is small [9, 183].

The central finding is the difference between doing better than a comparator and reaching an adequate level of recovery. For uncomplicated acute LBP, the natural-history evidence shows a mostly self-limiting course. Much of the recovery happens in the first several weeks, with no clear contribution from treatment. The treatment analyses give little evidence that any of the treatments speed this recovery. Every treatment, sham included, fell below natural history, with intervals that excluded zero. As discussed above, this more likely reflects differences between trial patients and natural-history cohorts than harm from treatment. In acute LBP, the key clinical question may not be whether patients improve with treatment. It may be whether treatment speeds recovery beyond what would happen anyway. Here, there was little evidence that it did.

In chronic LBP, SMT and exercise show the clearest added benefit over sham. Yet their average recovery remains below the 50% benchmark (SMT 31.8%; exercise 30.9%). That benchmark describes the population. It is not the chance that any one patient will benefit from treatment.

A descriptive sensitivity analysis of studies that enrolled mixed acute and chronic patients did not show results falling consistently between the acute and chronic estimates. This supports assigning studies to a phase, rather than treating mixed enrollment as a separate phase.

This analysis tackles the problem directly. It uses a natural-history estimate built separately from the treatment network (Paper I). It treats that estimate as uncertain rather than fixed. That uncertainty is then carried through the treatment analysis.

Splitting acute from chronic LBP is not just a convenience. It reflects two different background processes, which are described in Paper I.

Placebo Responsiveness

Sham meant a placebo procedure or a treatment known to be ineffective. We separate the sham procedure from the placebo response, which is the patient's response to receiving it.

Improvement seen with sham has two parts: the natural course of LBP, and the response to the sham. We therefore estimated placebo responsiveness as sham minus natural history. By removing the improvement predicted from independent natural-history evidence, this gives a cleaner estimate of the placebo response than raw improvement on sham.

A simple example makes the point. Suppose 68 of 100 sham-treated patients recover. Suppose natural history predicts that 60 of 100 similar patients would have recovered anyway (hypothetical values). Most of the sham result then reflects the natural course. Only the difference, 8 per 100, is due to receiving sham in a clinical setting. Calling 68 per 100 the placebo effect would overstate it more than eightfold. This is the difference between improvement in a placebo group and the placebo effect itself [9, 183].

Placebo responsiveness happens within the patient. It is not a property of the sham. Expectation, the patient-provider relationship, reassurance, attention, conditioning, the ritual of treatment, and provider interaction may all play a part. This analysis does not try to separate them. More broadly, placebo responsiveness has been proposed as an evolved capacity. In this view, cues from the environment and from other people can change the timing or size of the body's own responses to illness, pain, and recovery. Humphrey suggested that this responsiveness may help the body manage costly physical resources. Trimmer and colleagues later formalized this idea in evolutionary models [184] [185] [186] [187].

This analysis does not test that evolutionary idea. Instead, by separating natural-history improvement from the extra response seen with sham, it gives an empirical estimate of placebo responsiveness. It does not say how that responsiveness arises.

Extensive Overlap Among Conservative Treatments

A key feature of this analysis is how much the main treatment categories overlap once uncertainty is considered. The absolute recovery estimates and the relative effects tell the same story. SMT and exercise tend to sit near the top of the chronic group. But the gaps among active treatments are small compared with the uncertainty and the differences between studies.

Point estimates and rankings can make small differences look bigger than they are [188]. In acute LBP, the key feature is that treatment-versus-sham effects cluster tightly around zero, against a very favorable natural course. In chronic LBP, SMT and exercise show the clearest effects beyond sham. But the other active treatments overlap widely, and even the top two overlap each other. A consistent numerical order is not evidence that one treatment is meaningfully better.

The evidence supports a firmer conclusion about the difference between prognosis and treatment effect than about the exact order of treatments. In chronic LBP, SMT and exercise are the only active treatments with clearly positive effects versus sham in the current run. The evidence is less clear for medical care, modalities, and self-care. This is a narrower claim than saying that all structured conservative care reliably beats natural history or sham.

Between-Study Heterogeneity

Differences between studies remained large. This is not surprising, given how varied the LBP literature is. Studies differ in which patients they enroll, how severe and how long-lasting their pain is, how much treatment they give, how providers behave, how the comparator is designed, when outcomes are measured, how well the study is done, and how outcomes are measured.

This variation is informative. When differences between studies are large compared with differences between treatments, trials can honestly reach different answers. One does not have to be "right" and the other "wrong." Each is observing the treatment effect in a different clinical and research setting.

Standardized numbers are easier to judge when turned back into pain points. In our setup, 1 g equals about 2.0 NRS points. In acute LBP, the SD of study-level improvement was τ = 0.627 g, so about 95% of studies' underlying improvement lies within roughly two τ of the average. By comparison, the acute SMT-versus-sham effect was g = 0.09. The spread between studies is thus many times larger than the treatment difference we are trying to detect. That is why individual trials can disagree without any of them being wrong [189].

Standard heterogeneity statistics show that variation exists, but not where it comes from. The hierarchical model used here separates study-level variation from treatment effects. At the same time, it takes the expected natural course into account. The results suggest that much of the apparent disagreement about SMT may instead reflect differences in study populations, timing, sham conditions, and other design features.

Network Assumptions and Consistency

Overall, the network checks supported interpreting the NMA estimates within each phase.

Exchangeability should be seen as conditional, not absolute. Measured effect modifiers overlapped enough to combine studies. But leftover heterogeneity and thin evidence for some comparisons call for caution. Direct and indirect estimates generally agreed. Where they disagreed or evidence was thin, we interpreted the network estimates more cautiously. The network estimates are best read as average effects across varied but reasonably comparable studies. They are not effects that will apply everywhere.

Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Two conclusions in this paper rest on this logic.

A provider estimate whose interval includes zero does not show that providers are equivalent. A node split that finds no inconsistency does not show that direct and indirect evidence agree. In both cases, the interval may simply be too wide to reveal a real difference. Equivalence can be claimed only when the whole credible interval falls inside a preset zone of no practical importance, such as the ±0.30 zone used here [170, 190].

Study Quality and Blinding

Study quality may still help explain why LBP studies differ. Clinicians who deliver hands-on treatment usually cannot be blinded, and convincing patient blinding can be hard. In our models, higher-quality acute studies showed more improvement across all arms, while the chronic PEDro term was small and uncertain. Because the term shifts whole studies, it does not by itself explain differences between treatments.

PEDro is a combined quality score, not a pure measure of blinding. So these results cannot show which design features, if any, affect treatment effects. Because treating clinicians cannot be blinded, the provider's interaction with the patient is bound up with many hands-on treatments.

This makes credible sham procedures, matched for attention, especially valuable when the question is the specific effect of manipulation.

Clinical Interpretation

The evidence is clearest for acute LBP. No treatment studied, SMT included, added a meaningful benefit over sham, and no treatment arm recovered more often than natural history.

For uncomplicated acute LBP, the evidence therefore supports watchful waiting: reassurance, advice to stay active, and a supportive clinical relationship, with reassessment if recovery stalls or warning signs appear. Because LBP is among the costliest conditions in health care, routinely front-loading treatment in acute LBP spends resources where natural recovery is already strong [2]. Chronic LBP is different. There, SMT added about 13 recoveries per 100 patients at 54 weeks beyond both sham (+13.4; 95% interval +4.3 to +21.9) and natural history (+13.8; +4.3 to +22.6), and exercise added a similar amount over sham (+12.5; +5.5 to +20.4).

In chronic LBP, natural improvement is slower and overall recovery is lower. Yet SMT and exercise show clearer added benefit over sham. The clinical question therefore shifts. It is no longer whether patients improve, but how much extra benefit comes from the chosen treatment.

The sham experience may still differ across trials.

In uncomplicated acute LBP, fast expected recovery should be central to how results are read.

Our results support reassuring patients about their outlook and managing them conservatively.

They give little overall evidence that any of the treatments studied changes the underlying recovery path. This does not mean treatment can never relieve symptoms or suit an individual patient. It means that improvement after treatment should not, by itself, be taken as proof that treatment caused or sped up recovery [16, 191, 192].

Because active treatments overlap so much, choosing a treatment for chronic LBP can reasonably weigh safety, cost, access, patient preference, and burden. It can also weigh how well a treatment encourages activity and self-management. Small differences in average effectiveness need not be the only guide.

The cost and risk of needless clinical care. Treatment costs do not end with the fee. The average US trip for medical care is about 10 road miles each way [193], and an ambulatory visit takes about 121 minutes, 37 of them traveling and 84 in the clinic [194]. A course of 12 visits therefore adds about 240 miles and 24 hours. Vehicle operating costs at the IRS medical mileage rate of $0.235 per mile add about $56 [195]. External costs of driving, including congestion, local air pollution, and crash risk, add about $39 at $0.163 per mile [196] (in 2026 dollars).

Patient time, valued at about $66 per visit [194](in 2026 dollars), adds about $797. Together these come to roughly $875-$965 per course, depending on whether the patient lives in an urban or a rural area, before any fee is paid. Adding the mean amount paid per chiropractic visit in national survey data, about $114 in 2026 dollars ($84.84 in 2018 dollars) [197], brings the total to roughly $2,240-$2,330 per course.

Treatment also carries iatrogenic risk. Minor, transient adverse events, such as soreness or increased pain, follow spinal manipulation in about half of patients [198]. Serious events after lumbopelvic manipulation, including cauda equina syndrome, disc herniation, and fracture, are known only from case reports, so their incidence cannot be estimated, although it is thought to be very low [199]. Every comparator carries its own risks; neither medical care nor sham is riskfree.

At the population level, the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey records about 31-44 million chiropractic visits each year by US adults linked to low back conditions [200]. Because many chiropractic visits carry no coded musculoskeletal diagnosis, the true number is probably higher.

Fees, travel, externalities, and patient time for these visits total about $6-8.5 billion annually A main strength of this study is that it keeps natural-history evidence separate from the treatment network. Rather than assuming a fixed natural course, we imported an independent naturalhistory estimate (Paper I). We then carried its uncertainty into the treatment comparisons.

A second strength is that we report both absolute and comparative results. Treatment versus natural history asks whether improvement exceeds the expected course of the condition.

Treatment versus sham asks whether a treatment adds benefit beyond the sham experience.

Recovery probabilities describe how many patients are modeled to reach a meaningful outcome.

These are different questions. Looking at them together guards against two errors. A high recovery rate is not mistaken for a large treatment effect. And a real added effect in chronic LBP is not dismissed just because many patients still do not fully recover.

Other strengths include separate acute and chronic analyses, explicit study-level random effects, checks of transitivity and exchangeability, sensitivity analyses of recovery definitions and natural-history models, assessment of study quality, and an audit that kept the natural-history evidence independent of the treatment network. We also displayed full distributions, so that overlap between treatments could be judged directly rather than from point estimates or rankings alone.

Limitations

This study has several important limitations. First, the imported natural-history estimate shares the limitations of its evidence base, which are described in Paper I.

Second, natural-history cohorts, randomized trial populations, and observational treatment cohorts were not randomized against each other. So they cannot be assumed to be fully comparable. Observational cohorts were included only when their population, outcomes, timing, clinical phase, and source supported the role they played. Study-level random effects and measured study features reduce leftover differences but cannot remove them. Observational cohorts were never used in place of randomized treatment comparisons.

Third, sham procedures and trial settings varied across studies, even though sham was limited to placebo procedures or treatments known to be ineffective. This variation limits what the sham-minus-natural-history placebo estimate can tell us about mechanisms.

Fourth, putting different pain scales on a common footing requires assumptions. The conversion to recovery probability is easy to interpret clinically. But it depends on the chosen threshold and on assumptions about how individual changes are distributed. We used sample-size-weighted baseline means for each phase (4.823 acute; 5.284 chronic) and a fixed SD_NRS of 2.0. These gave thresholds of Δ = 1.412 and 1.642. We treated these values as fixed, not as uncertain.

Testing other recovery definitions reduces, but cannot remove, our reliance on the chosen threshold and conversion. In chronic LBP, the alternative recovery definitions were applied as threshold shifts relative to the favorable-course anchor, so those sensitivity results are approximate.

Fifth, the treatment trials mostly enrolled patients who could walk and attend outpatient care.

Patients with very severe pain, major loss of function, inability to walk, worsening nerve damage, or other conditions that rule out outpatient trials may be under-represented. These estimates should be applied cautiously to more severe or non-ambulatory patients.

Sixth, study quality was rated once per study, with AI assistance, and the ratings were not validated against human reviewers.

Seventh, treatment effects were assumed constant over time. Trial follow-up was short relative to the 26-and 54-week horizons, so absolute comparisons with natural history at those horizons are extrapolations. The common-asymptote and free-ceiling sensitivity analyses test other time shapes.

Finally, this is a study-level synthesis. Patient characteristics that may change response cannot be properly studied without individual participant data. Individual participant data meta-analyses of SMT in chronic LBP have begun to address this [201, 202]. Overlap in average treatment effects does not mean that all patients respond the same way. Nor does it rule out useful subgroups of patients who respond differently.

Implications for Future Research

Future LBP trials could be far more informative if they were designed around three things: natural recovery, the general effects of receiving care, and the specific effects of treatment.

In acute LBP, researchers should remember that treatment is being judged against a fastchanging background. Outcome times should be set in advance with expected natural recovery in mind. Claims that a treatment speeds recovery should require designs that can separate its effect from that background.

When the aim is to test a specific treatment mechanism, sham conditions should match provider contact, expectation, visit frequency, and other features of care as closely as possible. Comparing a hands-on treatment with an untreated waitlist cannot tell whether any difference comes from the procedure or from the clinical visit.

Future natural-history studies would also benefit from standard pain measures and repeated measurements starting close to symptom onset. They should record any treatment patients receive during follow-up. They should report enough data to estimate both the average course and its uncertainty. Individual participant data would allow more direct modeling of how recovery varies, and of possible subgroups that respond differently.

Finally, comparative-effectiveness studies should report uncertainty and overlap, not just treatment rankings. When several treatments have largely overlapping results, it may be more useful to find the safest, least burdensome, and most acceptable way to deliver the helpful parts of care they share. That may matter more than chasing small differences in average effect.

The clinical decision is not which treatment ranks first. It is whether the leading treatment helps enough to justify its use. In chronic LBP, SMT and exercise show added benefit over sham. Even so, their average recovery stays below 50% at 54 weeks. The analysis does not identify the individual practitioner as the active ingredient. Practitioner, patient, technique, and their interactions all remain possible sources of variation. Sorting them out will require linked data and replication.

Conclusion

This analysis separates the large improvement seen during treatment from the added benefit of treatment over a comparator. In acute LBP, natural recovery was favorable, and treatment showed little reliable advantage over sham. In chronic LBP, SMT and exercise showed the clearest added effects over sham. Even so, their modeled recovery stayed below 50% (31.8% and 30.9%). These findings call for a more cautious view of what treatment specifically achieves.

Care that adds nothing to natural recovery is not free: in acute LBP, travel, patient time, fees, and iatrogenic risk are incurred without additional benefit, at roughly $2,240-$2,330 per 12-visit course. These costs are part of the roughly $6-8.5 billion spent each year on US chiropractic visits for low back conditions. Differences between individual patients and between practitioners remain unresolved.

These findings may explain a long-standing feature of the SMT literature. Repeated trials have produced estimates that are often small, inconsistent, and frustratingly unstable. The treatment signal must be found against large natural improvement, placebo responsiveness, and differences between studies. When improvement in the comparison arm is high, the sample needed to detect a fixed treatment advantage grows steeply: with 59% improving on active treatment, about 72 participants are needed if 24% improve on placebo, but about 366 if 44% do [203]. Against that background, small differences in patients, comparators, follow-up, and design can change the observed result. Repeating the same kind of study therefore does not necessarily settle the question. More unstable estimates can make the literature bigger without making the treatment effect clearer. Future SMT research may be more useful if it is designed to separate treatmentspecific benefit from natural history and the general response to care. Simply adding more conventional comparisons to an already large evidence base is unlikely to help.

"Treatment works" is an incomplete scientific statement unless we say compared with what [38].

Estimating the expected course independently does not replace randomized evidence. It changes the question we can ask of it. The question moves from "Did patients improve?" to "How much better did patients do than we would otherwise have expected?" Future research should focus on questions that could change clinical decisions. Formal value-ofinformation analysis could test whether reducing the remaining uncertainty is worth more trials.

Studies that link patients to practitioners could look for consistent differences in how patients respond.

From the "tic" to the "tor"

Chiropractic has long distinguished between the "'tic," meaning the profession or system of care, and the "'tor," meaning the individual chiropractor. Putting the profession first implies a clinical product that can be transferred from one practitioner to another. If so, its benefits should be reproducible across practitioners.

This pooled evidence cannot show whether the practitioner, the technique, patient characteristics, or their interactions explain the leftover variation. Answering that will need data that link patients to practitioners, with enough replication to estimate each source of variation. An explanation based on the individual practitioner remains possible, but it has not been tested.

Under our model, outcome definition, and clinical benchmark, the evidence does not reliably show a general, clinically meaningful benefit specific to SMT as a category. This does not show that all effects of manipulation are zero. Nor does it show that individual practitioners cannot achieve good results, or that a professional title marks an effective ingredient. The roles of patient, practitioner, technique, and context remain unresolved.

The value of more conventional trials should be judged by the decisions they could change.

Formal value-of-information analysis could weigh the expected benefit of reducing uncertainty against research costs. Without such an analysis, this study cannot measure the cost or futility of further research.

the validation checks, and the uncertainty. This paper imports those results unchanged. The natural-history posteriors from Paper I enter this paper as external prior distributions for the background trajectory. They are not updated by the treatment trials; their uncertainty is propagated into every treatment estimate. An audit confirmed that no treatment trial fed into the Paper I model. It also confirmed that no prognosis cohort was treated as an arm in our network. The 26-week (acute) and 54-week (chronic) time points are when we compare treatments. They do not limit which prognosis studies Paper I could use. Treatment effects relative to natural history and sham For each phase, we modeled the standardized improvement in each treatment arm. The model accounts for four sources of variation. These are the uncertainty within each observation, extra unexplained scatter, differences between studies, and the structure of the treatment network. At the final step, we paired draws from the Paper I natural-history posterior with draws from the treatment posterior. Natural history is therefore an outside reference for "what would have happened anyway." It is not an extra node in the network. We formed a recovery comparison only after confirming that natural history and treatment measured the same outcome, or were linked by a measurement model set out in advance. Figure 1.

Figure 1. Treatment evidence networks for acute and chronic low back pain. Node size reflects the number of patients at the first reported time point. Node labels give the number of arms. Line width and line labels give the number of analytic units that compared each pair of treatments head-to-head. Sham is the comparator category. Arms from multi-arm studies can contribute to more than one pair.

Figure 2.

Figure 2. Direct versus indirect evidence for treatment comparisons. Random-effects node splitting compares direct and indirect estimates at preset time points for each phase. Only comparisons with both kinds of evidence are shown. We consider the size and uncertainty of any disagreement, not P values alone.

Figure 3.

Figure 3. Natural-history and treatment trajectories. Natural-history curves come from Paper I.

assumption. The model treats each treatment's effect as a constant shift from the natural-history curve. Yet the acute trial observations average only 7.1 weeks of follow-up, and the chronic observations 13.1 weeks against a 54-week horizon. Estimates at 26 and 54 weeks therefore carry that shift beyond most of the trial data; in Figure 3, panel C, each acute curve turns dotted where its trials end. Comparisons with sham are less affected, because sham and active arms share the same time structure. A sensitivity analysis that lets treatments change the rate of recovery, rather than shift it, is reported below.

Figure 4.

Figure 4. Clinical and standardized treatment effects. Acute and chronic results in clinical units are shown against the Paper I natural-history estimates. The standardized comparisons within the network can be read on their own, without the outside natural-history reference.

Figure 5

Figure5asks whether the advantage of each treatment depends on how we define a meaningful outcome. For each active treatment, it plots the difference from sham in recovery probability under four definitions: any improvement, at least 30% reduction, at least 50% reduction, and pain ≤2/10. In acute LBP, treatment-versus-sham differences stayed close to zero under every definition. In chronic LBP, SMT and exercise stayed above sham under all four definitions, with every 95% interval above zero. Medical care, modalities, and self-care had intervals that included zero under all four. For chronic LBP, the alternative definitions were applied as threshold shifts relative to the favorable-course anchor, so they are approximate. Figure5 thus

Figure 5 thus tests how robust the treatment-versus-sham comparison is. It does not test absolute recovery.

Figure 5.

Figure 5. Sensitivity of treatment advantage to the definition of a meaningful outcome. For each active treatment, points show the posterior mean number of extra recoveries per 100 compared with sham, under four recovery definitions. Bars are 95% credible intervals. Acute estimates are at 26 weeks and chronic estimates at 54 weeks. The zero line means no advantage over sham. Sham is the reference and is not plotted.

Figure 6.

Figure 6. Sensitivity of acute treatment effects to the natural-history functional form. Standardized treatment effects versus NMA sham (g; posterior mean and 95% credible interval) under the primary saturating natural-history trajectory and under the Bayesian linear trajectory (Table9).

Figure 5

Figure 5 asks whether the treatment-minus-sham difference holds up under other definitions of a meaningful outcome. In acute LBP, background recovery is strong and treatment adds little. In chronic LBP, the outlook is worse overall, but SMT and exercise show clearer added benefit over sham.

the linked Paper I posterior. Chronic natural-history sensitivity, validation against sources, and decisions about outcome types belong to Paper I. This paper reports sensitivity within the treatment network and what happens when other approved Paper I posteriors are imported.

2026 dollars). In acute LBP, where no treatment outperformed natural history, this spending buys no recovery beyond what natural history already provides. In chronic LBP, SMT's added benefit over sham of about 13 recoveries per 100 patients implies roughly $17,000 per additional recovery, counting all costs (about $10,200-$54,200 across the 95% interval).
